body.text: Attribution: Rahul Rawat, Ed., “China-Pakistan Military-Strategic Collusion: Capabilities, Functions, and Implications for India,” ORF Special Report No. 325, Observer Research Foundation, October 2026.

In what ways and to what extent do China and Pakistan, both nuclear-armed, collude against New Delhi?[1] This report explores the policy dimension of the much-debated question: why and how India became locked in a structural rivalry, as well as in a triadic relationship, with China and Pakistan.[2] The China-India-Pakistan relationship is marked by rivalry, asymmetry, and managed restraint. As three nuclear-armed states, the triadic relationship has both regional and global implications.

The four-day crisis in May 2025 was only the latest episode with evident elements of a military-strategic collusion between China and Pakistan against India. The episode resurfaced the complex reality that the interrelationship among China, India, and Pakistan is part of a structural triadic rivalry. The China-Pakistan relationship has transformed into a multi-domain cooperation and is often described as a ‘no-limits’ partnership in South Asia. As a means of deepening alignment,[a] China and Pakistan share military capabilities and technology, and co-produce major defence systems, in addition to contributing to the validation and development of doctrinal and warfighting elements. This also accommodates carefully managed, ambiguity-based engagement in the absence of a formal written alliance framework.

According to currently available information in the public domain, the alignment falls short of establishing access, a joint command, and explicit joint planning vis-à-vis India. Primarily, the contours of this short-of-formal-alliance include arms transfers, building of military capabilities, training, logistics, and planning. From India’s security calculus, the challenge of a China-Pakistan ‘threshold alliance’ manifests at the strategic and operational levels of war. In terms of planning and strategic assessments, New Delhi faces the challenge that lies somewhere between a two-front war as a worst-case scenario and a one-front reinforced war as the new reality. Operation Sindoor has opened a pandora's box on how and to what extent China-Pakistan military-strategic collusion is and would be functional against India in both peacetime and future crisis episodes.

This report examines the domain, range, and scope of collusion between China and Pakistan at the tactical, operational, and strategic levels, driven and facilitated by their political alignment vis-à-vis India. Here, the collusivity is measured by the development and transfer of operational military capabilities, planning, and the functioning of the armed forces of China and Pakistan. To this end, an empirical assessment of China-Pakistan cooperation is essential to measure the nature and character of their collusion against India.
Each chapter in this special report is designed to answer three interrelated questions in each domain and issue area:
• What kind of tangible and intangible capabilities are developed and transferred between China and Pakistan?
• How do these capabilities aim to enhance the domain-specific functions vis-à-vis India?
• What challenges and implications does it pose for India?

The report is divided into two sections: the first deals with China-Pakistan military-to-military cooperation across land, air, sea, cyber, space, Electronic Warfare (EW), and air defence elements, which support warfighting doctrine and military strategy; and the second examines how the China-Pakistan military-strategic alignment operates in real time across several thematic areas, including defence industrial and supply chains, intelligence and counterintelligence, the military grey zone, information, terrorism and counterterrorism, nuclear issues, planning, and interoperability. Each chapter provides an assessment of capabilities, doctrinal and operational collusion across the associated functions of China-Pakistan military-strategic alignment vis-à-vis India.

The China-Pakistan military-strategic collusion poses four types of threats or challenges for India. At one end of the spectrum lies a capabilities enhancement for Pakistan, ensured through strategic support from China. China's transfer of arms and military capabilities results in two levels of coercion[b] against India. Amidst existing Chinese capabilities aimed at coercing India to challenge its territorial status quo, Pakistan is being militarily empowered to challenge New Delhi. The second form of collusive threat is that China and Pakistan both challenge India in the grey zone in a near-simultaneous manner across the military and information domains. The third case is in the area of diplomatic and material support by Beijing to Islamabad during a crisis episode with New Delhi. Such a condition creates a ‘one-front reinforced’ war. Finally, the worst-case yet plausible scenario in the future, wherein China and Pakistan jointly plan an attack on India’s sovereignty to coerce and extract political concessions and, more importantly, to alter the status quo in a drastic manner. This form of challenge has been characterised by the Indian military and strategic policymakers as a ‘two-front’ challenge.[c]

The report concludes that the history of bilateral cooperation between China and Pakistan, specifically against India, has materialised in three forms: peacetime transfer and co-production of military capabilities; a limited but strategic support from China to Pakistan, without being dragged into the subcontinent’s wars, aimed at bolstering Islamabad’s position against New Delhi—the end state is a one-front reinforced war; and a collusive character in the grey zone, via near-simultaneous activities, primarily through the limited use of kinetic military power to erode and continuously challenge India’s immediate and general deterrence posture.

In a public speech, India’s National Security Advisor (NSA) Ajit Doval has underscored that “India has two neighbours, both nuclear powers (which) share a strategic relationship and a shared adversarial view of India.”[3] The establishment of credible deterrence through India’s military strategy and warfighting capabilities, backed by political will, is a prerequisite for achieving its grand strategic objectives. India cannot, and should not, escape its preparations for a two-front war.

The proposition is to be endorsed by a two-level logic. First, it would help to bridge the gap between India’s existing capabilities and the changing security environment. Second, a two-front scenario-based planning helps India better integrate its resources and align its planning with a more threat-centric assessment to address its two perennial adversaries. The preparedness against a China-Pakistan collusion demands not only military measures but also non-military policy options, such as diplomatic measures and a whole-of-government approach. For New Delhi, the necessity of strategy is what the former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Aerospace Force commander, Amir Ali Hajizadeh (now deceased), once said: maintaining deterrence is like riding a bicycle: “You have to keep pedalling all the time, or else the bicycle will fall.”[4]

In the long-term, the essence of strategy for India can be summed up in the words of the poet Ramdhari Singh Dinakar: Kshama shobti us bhujang ko, jiske paas garal ho, uska kya jo dantheen vishheen, vineet, saral ho (Forgiveness is becoming of the serpent that’s got venom; None cares for the toothless, poisonless, kind, gentle one). For India to achieve its ambitions of becoming a prosperous nation, a prerequisite is maintaining a peaceful external environment.

Endnotes

[a] According to Michael Ward, an alignment is not signified by formal treaties, but is delineated by a variety of behavioural actions. It is a more extensive concept than alliance since it does not focus solely upon the military dimension of international politics. Degrees of alignments in political, economic, military, and cultural spheres present a multifaceted sculpture of national and supranational postures. See: Michael D. Ward, Research Gaps in Alliance Dynamics (Denver: University of Denver, 1982).

[b] Coercion through military assistance or arms transfers by one actor to a third party directed against an actor constitutes the foundational logic of two-level coercion. The ‘two-level coercion’ has implications for both general and immediate coercion simultaneously of the targeted state.
